name: Independent cryptic crossword, Penguin book 1 No 1

book.title: The Penguin Book of Independent Crosswords, volume 1

clue.text: Girl's racing programme in shed

blocks.note: Di is a short girl's name, here with the possessive 's
a race card lists the runners at a race meeting

explanation.surface: A girl keeps her racecard in the garden shed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shed' looks like a noun, the hut where the programme is kept, but it is the verb to throw away.
explanation.definitionFit: To shed something is to cast it off or get rid of it, the same as discarding it.

clue.text: W.G. Grace, for example, caught sort of square — trapped by opener

indicators.note: something trapped is held inside, so these letters sit within the following word

blocks.note: a door is what you open to get in
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
a T-square is a draughtsman's tool

explanation.surface: The great cricketer W.G. Grace caught out at square leg.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket words point at Grace's batting, but he was also a qualified medical doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: W.G. Grace qualified as a physician and practised medicine, so he is an instance of a doctor.

clue.text: Percolation produces spot on one side of leaf

blocks.note: to spot is to see
a leaf of a book has two pages, one on each side

explanation.surface: Water filtering through leaves a spot on one side of a leaf.
explanation.definitionFit: Seepage is liquid slowly oozing or leaking through a porous material, a percolating flow.

clue.text: Cover purchased in confidence

blocks.note: first meaning: insurance cover
second meaning: self-assured certainty

explanation.surface: Someone bought insurance cover secretly, in confidence.
explanation.definitionFit: Life assurance is a policy bought for financial protection; assurance also means poise and self-belief.

clue.text: These tokens of respect indicate sod has been turned over

indicators.note: turned over like soil dug with a spade, the letters are churned into a new arrangement

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Turned turf at a memorial shows tributes have been paid.
explanation.walkthrough: Sod is turf, which fits 'turned over' as digging, but it is just fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Dedications are inscriptions honouring someone, at the front of a book or on a monument, marks of esteem.

clue.text: Came across cold tea being brewed

indicators.note: brewing stirs ingredients together, so the letters are mixed into a new order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone stumbled upon a pot of cold tea still brewing.
explanation.definitionFit: Having found something by chance or search, you have come across it; past tense synonym.

clue.text: Open country in Little America

indicators.note: in says the letters wanted sit inside the words that follow, across their join

blocks.note: the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: Wide open spaces found in a district called Little America.
explanation.definitionFit: A lea is a poetic word for meadow or grassland, open ground used for pasture.

clue.text: Plants behave unnaturally in Channel Islands

indicators.note: in places one set of letters inside the abbreviation that follows

blocks.note: CI is the abbreviation for the Channel Islands
to act is to put on a performance, behaving unnaturally

explanation.surface: Garden plants grow strangely on Jersey and Guernsey.
explanation.walkthrough: The Channel Islands, such as Jersey and Guernsey, lie off the French coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Cacti are spiny desert succulents, a family of flowering plants, plural of cactus.

clue.text: Fury over a paint in emulsion form

blocks.note: a temper is a fit of rage
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone raging about a pot of emulsion paint.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' puts the first part above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Tempera is a painting medium in which pigment is bound with egg yolk, an emulsion.

clue.text: Catastrophe for Kipling impostor

blocks.note: first meaning: a calamity
second meaning: in Kipling's poem If, Triumph and this are called two impostors

explanation.surface: A con man brings ruin to Rudyard Kipling.
explanation.walkthrough: Kipling's If— says 'meet with Triumph and Disaster, and treat those two impostors just the same'.
explanation.definitionFit: A disaster is a sudden calamity or ruinous event, and one of the two impostors named in Kipling's poem.

clue.text: This old timer could have trouble with the waterworks

definitions.text: This old timer could have trouble with the waterworks

blocks.clueFragment: This old timer could have trouble with the waterworks
blocks.note: surface reading: an elderly man with a bladder complaint
setter's reading: an ancient clock that measures time by water running out, which could fail if the flow goes wrong

explanation.surface: An elderly man suffers from bladder problems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old timer' is not an old man but an ancient timepiece, and its 'waterworks' are literal: it ran on dripping water.
explanation.definitionFit: A clepsydra is the water clock of antiquity, which tells time by the steady flow of water from a vessel.

clue.text: University powerless to produce French novelist

indicators.note: read as power-less, meaning without power, so the abbreviation for power is taken out

blocks.note: a campus is the grounds of a university, standing for it; P is the physics symbol for power

explanation.surface: A university suffers a power cut and somehow yields a French writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Split 'powerless' into power + less: CAMPUS loses its P to leave CAMUS.
explanation.definitionFit: Albert Camus wrote The Outsider and The Plague, novels of the French existentialist tradition.

clue.text: Rapturous broadcasting

blocks.note: first meaning: as in walking ..., overjoyed
second meaning: being transmitted live on radio or television

explanation.surface: A broadcaster is thrilled to be presenting.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on air is going out live on radio; walking on air is an idiom for elation and delight.

clue.text: She cannot succeed alone

blocks.note: surface reading: a woman who needs help to achieve anything
setter's reading: succeed means inherit, and this woman shares the inheritance with another

explanation.surface: A woman who never manages to achieve anything without help.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Succeed' means come next in line, as an heir does, not achieve success.
explanation.definitionFit: A co-heiress is a female who inherits jointly with one or more others, sharing the estate.

clue.text: Upper circle right for this musical film?

blocks.note: first meaning: the fashionable upper class
second meaning: the 1956 musical film with Bing Crosby and Grace Kelly

explanation.surface: Seats in the theatre's upper circle are just right for watching a musical.
explanation.walkthrough: The upper circle is also a tier of theatre seats, which fits the musical surface.
explanation.definitionFit: High society is the wealthy elite social set, and the title of a 1956 Cole Porter musical film.

clue.text: Teller of current bank accounts?

blocks.note: surface reading: a bank cashier handling current accounts
setter's reading: tales of animals living on the bank of a river, whose current flows past

explanation.surface: A bank cashier who deals with customers' current accounts.
explanation.walkthrough: A teller is also a storyteller; the bank is a riverbank and the accounts are stories, as in The Wind in the Willows with Ratty and Mole.
explanation.definitionFit: Kenneth Grahame wrote The Wind in the Willows, stories of animals living along a riverbank.

clue.text: Reduction found in a bargain department

blocks.note: taken as written
department stores traditionally sold cut-price goods in the basement

explanation.surface: Price reductions are to be had in a store's bargain department.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reduction' suggests a sale price, but it means being humbled.
explanation.definitionFit: Abasement is lowering in rank or dignity, a humbling reduction in status.

clue.text: Chinese white, for example?

blocks.note: surface reading: Chinese white, a white pigment used by painters
setter's reading: a person of mixed Asian and European descent

explanation.surface: An artist names a white watercolour pigment.
explanation.walkthrough: Chinese white is a zinc oxide paint, but read the two words as two ancestries.
explanation.definitionFit: Eurasian describes a person with one European and one Asian parent, such as Chinese and white.

clue.text: Liberating tales from Wodehouse, say, in America

blocks.note: first meaning: an abolitionist novel that helped turn opinion against slavery
second meaning: Uncle Tom Travers is Bertie Wooster's uncle in Wodehouse, and an American would call a humble house a cabin

explanation.surface: Stories of escape taken from P.G. Wodehouse, set in the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half is cryptic: the house of a Wodehouse uncle, named in American terms, as though Wodehouse were split into its parts.
explanation.definitionFit: Harriet Beecher Stowe's novel attacked slavery and was credited with fuelling the movement to free slaves.

clue.text: Sword-clash sound a common mistake, we hear

indicators.note: we hear says the word is identified by how it is spoken, not spelt

blocks.note: a clanger is a blunder, British slang

explanation.surface: The clash of swords comes from a common mistake, apparently.
explanation.walkthrough: Dropping a clanger is British slang for making an embarrassing blunder.
explanation.definitionFit: Clangor, or clangour, is a loud ringing metallic noise, like blades striking each other.

clue.text: Delivery-variation for striker to watch

blocks.note: surface reading: a change in how something is delivered that a striker must look out for
setter's reading: the batsman facing in cricket must watch a ball that curves in toward him

explanation.surface: A footballer must watch for a different kind of cross.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the striker is the batsman on strike, and a delivery is one ball bowled.
explanation.definitionFit: An inswing is a bowled ball that curves in the air from off side toward the batsman's legs.

clue.text: Travelling-case, formerly a set of three

blocks.note: ex means former, as in ex-wife
a tern is a group of three, especially three lottery numbers

explanation.surface: A suitcase that once came in a set of three.
explanation.walkthrough: The case is not luggage but a medical case: a patient who comes in from outside.
explanation.definitionFit: An extern is a non-resident, such as an outpatient or day pupil who travels in rather than living there.

clue.text: Medical troubleshooter?

blocks.note: surface reading: someone who fixes problems in a hospital
setter's reading: something that shoots down trouble, here bodily pain

explanation.surface: An expert brought in to sort out problems in a hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'troubleshooter' literally as a thing that knocks out trouble, and the trouble is pain.
explanation.definitionFit: An analgesic is a painkilling drug, which relieves the discomfort a patient suffers.

clue.text: Scots regiment with slight injury reported

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so its spoken form counts

blocks.note: a graze is a scrape on the skin

explanation.surface: A soldier of a Scottish regiment has a minor wound.
explanation.walkthrough: The Royal Scots Greys were a famous Scottish cavalry regiment.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scots Greys, named for their grey horses, were a Scottish cavalry regiment of the British Army.

clue.text: The Queen's favourite county

blocks.note: first meaning: the Earl of ..., a favourite courtier of Elizabeth I
second meaning: an English county east of London

explanation.surface: Her Majesty's preferred English county.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one phrase; split it after 'favourite'. Robert Devereux, Earl of Essex, was Elizabeth I's favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: Essex is a county in eastern England, and the title of the earl who was Elizabeth's favourite.

clue.text: Fire leg-break after batting

indicators.note: to break something is to smash it apart, so its letters are scattered and reformed

blocks.note: in cricket the side batting is said to be in
the letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A spin bowler fires down a leg-break after the batsman has come in.
explanation.walkthrough: A leg-break is a spinning cricket delivery, but here leg is the fodder and break the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: An ingle is a fire on a domestic hearth, as in inglenook, the corner beside the fireplace.

clue.text: Head of English in prettier form of past tense

indicators.note: the head of a word is its leading letter, so only that one is kept
to form something is to shape it anew, so the letters are given a fresh order

blocks.note: its first letter
taken as written, to be mixed with the extra letter

explanation.surface: An English teacher dresses up the past tense more prettily.
explanation.definitionFit: Preterite is the grammarians' name for the simple past form of a verb, such as went or saw.

clue.text: Seed blown by the wind?

blocks.note: surface reading: a seed scattered by a breeze
setter's reading: the wind is a person's breath, puffing a small round seed through a shooter tube

explanation.surface: A seed carried away on the breeze.
explanation.walkthrough: Wind here is breath: children blow this seed through a tube, the shooter named after it.
explanation.definitionFit: The pea is a small round edible seed from a pod, ammunition for a schoolboy's shooter.

clue.text: Portia's attendant returning in role of seductress

indicators.note: returning means going back the way you came, so the letters are read from the end

blocks.note: as means in the role of, as in acting as
a siren is an alluring, dangerous woman

explanation.surface: Portia's maid comes back playing the part of a temptress.
explanation.walkthrough: Portia is the heroine of Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice.
explanation.definitionFit: Nerissa is Portia's waiting-woman in The Merchant of Venice, who disguises herself as a clerk.

clue.text: Weapon for any aga turning out to surround Turkish leader

indicators.note: turning something out means rearranging it, so the letters are shuffled
the rearranged letters wrap around another letter placed inside them
a leader goes at the front, so only the opening letter is taken

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged
its first letter

explanation.surface: A Turkish chief needs a weapon to deal with any Aga, a Turkish commander.
explanation.walkthrough: An aga is an Ottoman officer, which fits the Turkish scene nicely.
explanation.definitionFit: A yataghan or yatagan is a Turkish sabre with a curved blade and no guard.
